## What to look for

- How old is the Sun today? How much longer will it stay on the main sequence?
- When will Earth lose its oceans? Long before or after the Sun becomes a red giant?
- Which planets are swallowed by the red giant? Why do the orbits of the others widen?
- Follow the Sun's track on the small diagram: where does it end up, and why will it never explode as a supernova?

## How it works

The Sun slowly brightens as it turns hydrogen into helium. When the hydrogen of its core runs out, it swells into a red giant about 250 times its present size and loses much of its mass, so the planets' orbits widen. After the helium flash and a last swelling, it blows off its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf the size of Earth. The timeline is not to scale: the late stages are stretched to be visible.

## Sources

Model values after Sackmann, Boothroyd & Kraemer (1993), *Our Sun. III. Present and Future*, and Schröder & Smith (2008), *Distant future of the Sun and Earth revisited*.
